title: Fall in love with the problem, not the solution

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Here's a line Antoine still repeats from an entrepreneurship program: fall in love with the problem, not the solution.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like advice people hear and then ignore. What was the program?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: QcES, the Spring 2024 cohort. He took part while working through lean discovery: the business model canvas, customer interviews, short pitches. The post is his own recap, not an official document.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Start with the canvas. What's the point of it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nine blocks on one page, but the trick is you don't fill it in once and frame it. You state a hypothesis, talk to people, adjust the segments and the value proposition, then practice explaining it out loud. They pushed everyone to nail down who it's for and how you help before optimizing anything else.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He calls them the heart of the cohort. They're for learning, not closing a sale. Don't pitch your fix on the call. Ask how the other person lives the problem, and talk beyond your ideal customer: people using substitutes, experts, suppliers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: About ninety seconds, no slides. And a structure: Hook, Believe, Join. Hook with the problem and why it matters, not the product. Believe, with the solution and evidence. Join, with one specific ask, like money, expertise, or an introduction.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It forces clarity early. Same with the feedback rounds: name one real strength, then one concrete way to make it stronger.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. A proof of concept asks whether it can work. A prototype explores how people interact with it. An MVP is the smallest version you put in front of real users. Not the same thing.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A few well-run interviews teach more than a beautifully styled canvas. Consistency beats polish. The full write-up has a week-by-week table for a founder friend.
